item.title: Highways from the Silver Screen
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Seven iconic cinematic routes, from coastal backroads to cross-country detours.

There is a distinct geometry to the cinematic road trip. Long before turn-by-turn navigation smoothed over the friction of transit, putting characters on the open road forced them to confront raw distance, shifting topography, and each other. Unlike air travel, which erases the world between point A and point B, the road trip honors the transition. Across these seven journeys, the route itself becomes as essential to the narrative as the travelers behind the wheel.

For some, the road is a stage for family dynamics testing their limits across state lines. In National Lampoon’s Vacation, Clark Griswold herds his family from Chicago to Anaheim in a station wagon along Interstate 40 and historic Route 66. The journey’s defining visual remains the dusty, sprawling expanse of Monument Valley along the Utah-Arizona border—a magnificent backdrop that contrasts sharply with their chaotic trek toward the locked gates of Walley World. Decades later, Little Miss Sunshine traced a similar western path along Interstate 10, carrying the fractured Hoover family from Albuquerque to Redondo Beach in a sputtering 1971 Volkswagen Microbus. The film’s most memorable stretch unfolds on the highway shoulder, where the family must run alongside the moving bus to jump through the sliding door—a physical manifestation of keeping a family moving forward despite mechanical failure.

In lighter territory, the road serves as the ultimate test of directional sense. Dumb and Dumber tracks an absurd cross-country haul from Providence, Rhode Island, to Aspen, Colorado. Its defining highway moment arrives when a wrong turn in Nebraska sends Lloyd and Harry driving for hours in the wrong direction across the freezing plains toward Kansas on a tiny moped—a hilarious, cautionary reminder of what happens when you abandon the map entirely.

For others, the highway provides space for quiet reflection and unexpected bonding. In Sideways, two friends take a battered Saab convertible from San Diego into the backroads of Santa Barbara County’s Santa Ynez Valley. Cruising along Foxen Canyon Road past golden, oak-studded hills and rolling vineyards, the landscape mirrors the slow pace of wine country and the quiet existential reckonings of midlife. Further east, Rain Man takes a deliberate detour as Charlie Babbitt drives his autistic savant brother, Raymond, from Cincinnati to Los Angeles in a 1949 Buick Roadmaster. By intentionally avoiding interstates for two-lane state highways and Route 66, the slow pace of the open road forces Charlie to adapt to Raymond’s unhurried rhythm, transforming a hostile drive into genuine connection.

The road also acts as a moving sanctuary for those seeking identity or escape. In Almost Famous, a young journalist joins the rock band Stillwater aboard their tour bus, “Doris,” tracing a hazy arc through the American Rust Belt and Midwest. The heart of the film rests in a late-night drive down a dark highway after a chaotic party, where the entire bus quietly sings along to Elton John’s “Tiny Dancer,” capturing the fleeting, sacred unity found only in transit.

At the far end of the spectrum, Into the Wild follows Christopher McCandless from Atlanta through the Southwest and Pacific Northwest, ending in the Alaskan interior. The journey culminates on the desolate, snow-dusted stretch of the Stampede Trail near Healy, Alaska, where the gravel peters out into pure wilderness—marking the final transition from the highway to complete isolation.

Whether navigating family chaos, rolling vineyards, or distant horizons, these seven films remind us of a fundamental travel truth: the moments that define a trip rarely happen at the destination—they happen along the way.

This piece is part of the latest issue of Curated Travel Magazine, where we explore travel through immersive stories, cultural insight, and thoughtfully curated experiences around the world.

item.title: The Journey to the World’s Northernmost Commercial Lodge
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At Nordenskiöld Lodge, reaching the destination is part of the experience. Set within the Arctic landscape of Spitsbergen, the remote lodge is the northernmost commercial lodge in the world and can only be reached by boat or snowmobile. In winter, Basecamp Explorer’s Glacier Odyssey turns the journey into a 100-kilometer expedition across snowy terrain, glaciers, frozen fjords and wind-carved valleys.

The lodge itself offers a striking contrast to the surrounding wilderness. Designed by Norwegian interior expert Halvor Bakke, its warm materials and colors frame views of the glacier, mountains and fjord, creating an intimate retreat within an otherwise immense landscape. After days spent crossing the Arctic by snowmobile, evenings center on communal dinners and time around the fire with the lodge host, sharing stories and knowledge of the region.

The Curated Take: Nordenskiöld Lodge is compelling because the Arctic isn’t simply scenery surrounding the hotel. The remoteness defines the experience from beginning to end. The 100-kilometer snowmobile journey makes arrival feel earned, while the lodge provides just enough warmth and intimacy to create a meaningful counterpoint to the wilderness outside.

item.title: A Winter Escape Where the Water Runs Warm
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
For travelers ready to leave winter behind entirely, Rio Perdido Hotel & Thermal River offers a very different kind of seasonal escape. Set within a wilderness landscape in Costa Rica’s Guanacaste region, the eco-luxury retreat combines outdoor adventure with the natural thermal waters of the volcanic landscape.

Days can move between hiking and mountain biking and experiences centered on the property’s thermal rivers and mineral pools, with volcanic mud adding another dimension to the retreat’s connection to the surrounding geology. Winter is particularly well suited to a Costa Rica escape, as the country’s dry season generally runs from mid-December through late April, bringing warm, sunny conditions to the outdoor landscape.

The Curated Take: Rio Perdido’s appeal is that wellness here begins with the landscape itself. Rather than separating adventure from relaxation, the retreat makes the volcanic environment the common thread, allowing travelers to move from an active day outdoors to naturally warm waters without leaving the setting that makes Guanacaste distinctive.

item.title: Valletta Offers a Warmer Take on the European Winter City Break
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
While Europe’s best-known winter city breaks tend to revolve around colder capitals and Christmas markets, Valletta offers a distinctly Mediterranean alternative. Malta’s capital combines mild winter weather with UNESCO-listed architecture, centuries of history, a growing culinary scene and a festive calendar that gives travelers plenty of reasons to explore beyond the summer season.

Iniala Valletta provides a particularly well-positioned base for experiencing the city. The hotel has introduced Solis, a collection of suites overlooking the Grand Harbour, while its two-MICHELIN-starred ION Harbour has recently been refurbished and a new dining concept, Anaalā, has joined the property’s culinary offering. The hotel’s winter programming also includes cultural, gastronomic and adventure experiences, including private access to St John’s Co-Cathedral. With fewer summer crowds, travelers can spend their days wandering Valletta’s historic streets, exploring the coast and venturing into surrounding towns at a more leisurely pace.

The Curated Take: Valletta makes sense as a winter destination precisely because it doesn’t try to recreate the traditional European winter city break. Its appeal is the combination of history, architecture, food and Mediterranean light, with winter offering a chance to experience one of Europe’s most atmospheric capitals without the intensity of its summer season.

item.title: A New Way to Experience Finnish Lapland
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Finnish Lapland is welcoming a new luxury base for experiencing its forests, frozen lakes and Arctic fells. Opening for its inaugural winter season in December 2026, Arcora Boutique Hotel & Villas is set in Torassieppi, Muonio, surrounded by the landscapes of Pallas-Yllästunturi National Park and a region known for exceptionally clean air.

The property will feature 59 boutique suites and Sky and Deluxe Villas, along with a restaurant inspired by Lapland’s eight seasons, an artisan bakery, champagne bar, spa with traditional saunas, and rooftop and infinity pool. The most distinctive element, however, may be Arcora’s private “By Owner” experiences, hosted by one of the Pietikäinen brothers, the third generation of the family behind Arcora and Harriniva Hotels & Safaris. Guests can travel by snowmobile across frozen lakes and fells, visit a family-connected reindeer estate, meet huskies or explore Pallas-Yllästunturi National Park by snowshoe, with the experiences shaped by generations of local knowledge.

The Curated Take: Arcora’s strongest point of difference is its connection to the people behind the property. The “By Owner” experiences turn familiar Lapland activities into opportunities to encounter the region through a family that has been part of its tourism story for decades. That connection gives the new hotel a sense of place that goes beyond the increasingly familiar formula of luxury Arctic accommodation.

item.title: Heritage in Motion
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
By rail into Britain’s West: Cornwall, Wales, and the Lakes

There is a quiet rhythm to the way landscape reveals itself from the window of a train. Unlike the abrupt transitions of air travel, rail demands an uninterrupted dialogue with time and terrain. As Curated Travel Magazine marks its first anniversary, we return to this foundational truth of travel: that the most profound journeys do not merely take us somewhere new, but carry us through layers of living history.

Entering this lineage is Belmond’s newest sleeper icon, the Britannic Explorer—the first luxury sleeper train to weave through England and Wales. Traversing three distinct geographical itineraries, the train serves as a moving gallery framing the deep-rooted heritage, regional provenance, and timeless spirit of Britain’s western realms.

Cornwall: Granite, Canvas, and Salt Air

To travel south toward the Cornish peninsula is to trace a landscape defined by industrial tenacity and artistic light. Crossing Isambard Kingdom Brunel’s 1859 Royal Albert Bridge over the River Tamar marks the threshold into Kernow.

Here, the track skirts wild Atlantic coastlines and dramatic granite cliffs crowned with the engine houses of 18th-century tin and copper mines. Beyond its rugged topography, Cornwall’s cultural heritage is bound to its light—a quality that famously drew mid-century modernist painters to St. Ives. The journey pauses for private tastings overlooking St. Michael’s Mount and curated access to Hauser & Wirth Somerset, connecting the region’s historic maritime heritage with its contemporary creative energy.

Wales: Slate, Song, and Mountain Sanctuaries

Heading northwest, the landscape shifts dramatically into Cymru, a realm where geography and identity are seamlessly intertwined. The route cuts through the heart of Eryri (Snowdonia) National Park, a terrain carved by ancient slate quarries that once roofed the Victorian world.

From the train’s observation car, the view unfolds in sweeping vistas of emerald valleys, ancient oak woods, and high mountain passes. The cultural texture here is palpable: passing coastal sanctuaries and historic slate towns, one senses a heritage preserved through the Welsh language, coastal folklore, and an enduring connection to the soil.

The Lake District: Fells, Poets, and Pastoral Roots

Climbing north toward Cumbria, the rail line crosses the monumental stone arches of the Ribblehead Viaduct along the Settle-Carlisle line—an engineering marvel of the 1870s. The scenery softens into the romantic, tarn-speckled fells of the Lake District, a UNESCO World Heritage site shaped by centuries of pastoral hill-farming and immortalized by Wordsworth and Coleridge.

Here, heritage is deeply agricultural. Off-train excursions take guests into historic estates like Graythwaite and the Cartmel Valley, where traditional Herdwick sheep farming continues on the same fells as it has for generations, sustaining an uninterrupted pastoral way of life.

Belmond’s Art of Continuation

Launching a new luxury train is a balance of innovation and homage. Drawing on a century of rail heritage—from the legendary Venice Simplon-Orient-Express—Belmond created the Britannic Explorer not as a retro museum piece, but as a modern interpretation of vintage rail glamour.

Designed by London-based studio Luke Edward Hall, the train’s interiors mirror the British landscape. Rich botanical palettes of deep blues and earth tones complement rattan panels and bespoke woodwork. The three Grand Suites—named after native flora Juniper, Valerian, and Elder—evoke the elegance of an English country house.

This philosophy extends directly to the dining cars, Malva and Samphire, overseen by chef Simon Rogan. Celebrated for his pioneer role in farm-to-table cuisine, Rogan’s menus are directly inspired by the train’s routes, featuring hyper-local Cumbrian produce, fresh Welsh sea salt, and seasonal Cornish seafood. It is an editorial approach to gastronomy: every meal reflects the exact coordinates outside the window.

As the Britannic Explorer glides along the rails, it carries forward a simple truth: the grandest journeys are those that connect where we are going with everything that came before.

item.title: Hotels Are Making Room for a New Kind of Guest: Gamers
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Hotels have long competed to make the guest room feel like a retreat, but nhow Hotels & Resorts is betting that some travelers want something very different: a place to play. The design-driven European brand has launched GAME:NXT by nhow, a new gaming and esports concept developed in partnership with SK Gaming that brings professional-grade digital experiences directly into the hotel stay.

Following a pilot at nhow Berlin, the concept is now expanding across Europe, with nhow Frankfurt the latest property to introduce dedicated Gaming Rooms. Six rooms feature high-performance PCs, ultra-fast connectivity, ergonomic gaming setups, dual high-resolution screens and PlayStation 5 consoles, with VR headsets and streaming equipment available on request. Guests can also request portable POGA Gaming Suitcases, which turn a conventional hotel room into a private gaming setup with a PlayStation 5, controllers and an integrated screen. The suitcases are now available at participating nhow properties in Germany, the BeNeLux, Italy and France, while Gaming Rooms are planned for nhow Amsterdam, Rotterdam and Brussels in 2027. A new Gaming Studio is also planned for nhow Brussels, following Berlin’s model as a space for content creators, esports teams and boot camps.

The Curated Take: GAME:NXT is interesting because it treats gaming as part of the culture of travel rather than simply another hotel amenity. For a generation accustomed to bringing entertainment, community and work into the hotel room through a laptop or phone, the next evolution may be hotels deliberately designing spaces around those digital identities. Nhow is essentially asking what a hotel room looks like when gaming is one of the reasons a guest wants to be there.

item.title: Savannah’s Bohemian Riverfront Hotel Finds a New Perspective
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Savannah’s riverfront is getting a new point of view. The former Bohemian Savannah Riverfront has become Hotel Orielle, an Autograph Collection Hotel, retaining its Marriott affiliation while introducing a new identity built around what it calls the “art of noticing.” The 75-room hotel takes its name from the 19th-century oriel window, a design element intended to offer a broader vantage point, and uses the idea of perspective as a thread through the guest experience.

That philosophy shows up in the details. Daily river and tide notes connect guests to the waterfront, live music encourages lingering, and a new art collection includes a three-panel mixed-media installation by SCAD alumna Lillian Blades inspired by the Lowcountry marshes, work by artist and former SCAD professor Katherine Sandoz, salon-style gallery installations and a 33-foot rooftop mural incorporating Savannah’s maritime history. At Rocks on the Roof, the city’s tallest rooftop along River Street, brass spyglass binoculars are placed throughout the space each evening at dusk, turning sunset into a ritual of looking more closely at Savannah. A new signature cocktail, The Orielle, accompanies the experience, while newly appointed executive chef Johnny Salaverria brings his Venezuelan roots and Savannah influences to Coastal 15 Fish House and the rooftop restaurant.

The Curated Take: Hotel Orielle is most interesting as an example of a hotel using design and ritual to change how travelers encounter a familiar destination. Rather than attempting to compete with Savannah’s history and architecture, the property is creating small prompts to make guests pay closer attention to them. The result is a hotel concept that feels particularly suited to a city whose character is often found in its quieter details.

item.title: Courmayeur’s Winter Goes Beyond the Slopes
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
At the foot of Mont Blanc, Courmayeur delivers the classic visual drama of an Italian Alpine winter, but the experience extends well beyond downhill skiing. Grand Hotel Courmayeur Mont Blanc provides a base for exploring the landscape by snowshoe and Nordic ski, while the Val Ferret offers another way to experience the mountains at a slower pace.

For a different perspective on the Alps, guests can ascend Skyway Monte Bianco for sweeping views of the surrounding peaks, or work with the hotel’s Ski Concierge to tailor time on the slopes. Afterward, the adults-only ERRE Spa offers a quieter counterpoint to the day’s outdoor adventures, creating a natural transition from mountain activity to recovery.

The Curated Take: Courmayeur’s appeal lies in the range of ways to experience the same landscape. Skiing may be part of the itinerary, but snowshoeing, Nordic skiing and the Skyway offer entirely different perspectives on Mont Blanc. It makes the destination particularly appealing to travelers who want an Alpine winter without spending every hour on a ski lift.

item.title: The Mallorca Most Travelers Miss
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Mallorca has a reputation for Mediterranean beaches and summer escapes, but winter reveals a quieter side of the island. At La Reserva Rotana, a private 200-hectare estate above Manacor, the experience shifts inland, into vineyards, almond and carob groves, woodland and organic farmland surrounding a reimagined historic manor house.

The slower winter season offers an opportunity to experience Mallorca through its countryside rather than its coastline. Guests can settle into the estate’s culinary offerings, explore local wines and spend time amid the agricultural landscape, where the pace is dictated less by the summer season and more by the rhythms of the land.

The Curated Take: La Reserva Rotana offers a compelling reminder that Mallorca is more than a beach destination. Winter makes the island’s rural character easier to appreciate, particularly for travelers drawn to food, wine, landscape and a sense of place rather than a traditional resort escape.
